source.title: The Illusion of Diminishing Returns: Measuring Long Horizon Execution in LLMs
source.authors: Akshit Sinha; Arvindh Arun; Shashwat Goel; S. Staab; Jonas Geiping

record.file_problem: none; full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures task performance across model sizes using a synthetic long-horizon execution benchmark. This bears on the qualitative downstream-performance-with-scale version, but it does not measure pretraining loss or fit the original loss-scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. when discussing diminishing returns in next-token loss, but reports no results measuring held-out cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute loss curves, extrapolation of loss fits, or compute-optimal allocations. Its own scale-related results measure execution accuracy and horizon length; those bear only on V6. Results about self-conditioning, thinking, and context management do not measure any other listed version.
record.test_reason: The paper's own results compare execution accuracy and horizon length across sizes within the Gemma3 and Qwen3 families on a new synthetic long-horizon task. That is a downstream-performance-with-scale result, so it bears on V6 in a new setting. It measures no pretraining loss, fits no curve, and allocates no compute, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that scaling model size increases the number of turns a model can execute and that sequential test-time compute increases steps per turn. They argue short-task benchmarks may give an illusion of diminishing returns. They also find that self-conditioning is not fixed by scale but is fixed by thinking. They explicitly decline to derive a scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a synthetic key-value retrieval and running-sum execution benchmark rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss or fitting parameter/token/compute loss laws.
record.method_sensitivity: For the execution results, the paper reports sensitivity to turn complexity, thinking or chain-of-thought, and context history; it also says temperature does not materially alter the observed trends. These are not tests of loss-law fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Self-conditioning, measured as accuracy loss at turn 100 when injected errors are placed in the history, does not shrink with scale. The authors say scaling size increases it, even in 200B+ models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling model size does not reduce error-conditioned degradation in long-horizon execution.

fits_no_version.finding: Analytical argument that small gains in step accuracy compound into hyperbolic growth in horizon length, so short-task metrics understate the benefit of scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Diminishing per-step returns can coexist with exponential gains in task horizon.

record.code_released: Complete source code and data generation scripts are stated to be included as supplementary material; URL not stated.
record.problems: The scale result uses a synthetic execution task and at most four model sizes per family; the authors explicitly decline to derive a scaling law. Most plotted results are not numerically tabulated in the text. The authors note that improvement on this task is necessary but not sufficient for long-horizon execution in real-world tasks.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were included: the paper’s self-conditioning, thinking, context-engineering, self-verification, and turn-complexity experiments do not measure any other listed claim version. Cited loss-scaling findings are not the paper’s own results.

untested.parts: Quantitative prediction or extrapolation from a fitted curve. Prediction from pretraining loss. Standard downstream benchmarks.
All parts: no held-out loss is measured.
All parts. The Qwen3-Next architecture remark concerns execution length, not loss at fixed size.

missing.what: Horizon length increases with model size when thinking/CoT is enabled at K=10, for both families.
Accuracy at turn 100 with an error-free (healed) history improves with model size, up to near-perfect for 200B+ frontier models.
Size trends are reproduced at temperature 0.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is a weak, qualitative test of V6: within-family size comparisons with three or four sizes, values readable only from figures. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as motivation. No result bears on the loss-based versions.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute; no loss curves are measured.
No small-run loss fit or prediction of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens, or fitted growth trends for either.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count for loss.
Thinking and chain-of-thought are evaluated for execution, not for whether loss power laws transfer across modalities or training regimes.

Tests qualitative execution-benchmark performance across model sizes, not standard downstream benchmarks, performance predicted from pretraining loss, or quantitative prediction/extrapolation from a fitted scaling curve.
No analysis of loss-law fitting choices, fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, or bending loss curves.

rows.subject: Gemma3 model-size sweep
rows.operation_detail: Compared task accuracy across model sizes on the long-horizon execution task with K=1.
rows.value: figure only; the text states that larger models sustain higher task accuracy for significantly more turns.
rows.uncertainty: mean ± one standard deviation over 100 samples
rows.note: Qualitative family size-scaling result reported in the text; the plotted individual values are not transcribed in the paper text.
rows.check: Baseline is the smaller models in the same family, not 'not stated'. The value is figure-only (Fig. 4c), so only the direction is readable. 'Predictably' is not tested: there is no fit.

relationships.condition: Gemma3 (4/12/27B) and Qwen3 (4/8/14/32B) on the synthetic key-value running-sum task. Holds at K=1 without thinking, and per the text also at K=10 with thinking/CoT.
relationships.reason: Larger models sustain task accuracy for more turns and horizon length rises with size (R1–R4). The K=10 thinking result comes from the text (Fig. 13d) and has no row. The evidence is directional only, with no fitted or predictive curve.
relationships.display_finding: Larger models maintained accuracy for more turns, both at K=1 without thinking and K=10 with thinking, without a fitted predictive curve.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma3 and Qwen3 size sweeps on the paper’s synthetic long-horizon execution task
reader_labels.reason: The text reports that larger models sustain higher task accuracy for more turns and that horizon length shows a clear scaling trend (R1–R4). This is qualitative evidence on this benchmark, not a fitted or extrapolative prediction.
